sentences: I count the five lines of the staff from bottom to top before I write the treble clef at the start.
I check the key signature for sharps or flats and apply them to every note unless an accidental overrides it.
I read the time signature to know how many beats each measure contains and which note value gets the beat.
I mark the rehearsal letters in the margins so I can find the same spot after a page turn.
I pencil in the fingering numbers above the notes when the printed edition leaves them out.
I erase the old pencil marks from the previous rehearsal before I write new bowings on the string parts.
I count the measures of rest and write the total number in the middle of the empty staff.
I follow the repeat signs to the beginning and play the section again without turning the page.
I locate the coda sign and jump to the coda when the conductor gives the cue.
I read the tempo marking at the top of the page and set the metronome to that number.
I observe the dynamic marks under the staff and adjust the volume of each phrase accordingly.
I check the slurs and ties to see which notes are connected and which are held over.
I read the articulation marks, such as staccato dots and accent wedges, above the notes.
I count the ledger lines above the staff to identify notes that are higher than the treble range.
I transpose the written part for my instrument by reading each note a whole step lower.
I turn the page at the rest in measure thirty-two to keep the music continuous.
I check the binding and tape any loose pages so they do not fall out of the folder.
I compare the printed score with the handwritten manuscript to see if the notes match.
I write the chord symbols above the staff for the guitarist to read during the performance.
I number the measures at the start of each line to make rehearsal directions easier to follow.
